summary:
Ben Kus, CTO of Box, frames Box's scale (over an exabyte of data, tens of millions of users, hundreds of billions of content objects, and now a roughly one-trillion-token AI workload heading to ten trillion) and walks through prior technology waves (internet, mobile, cloud) where the durable enterprise playbook was to pick a stack, get good at it, and optimize it, because foundational infrastructure like HTTP, iOS, and Android persisted. He argues that playbook is now breaking under AI because the rate of change is dramatically higher: almost every layer powering generative AI is in flux.

He retracts his own AI Engineer talk from the prior year, which recommended a graph-based approach to agents, and now wonders how the attendee who thanked him fared when a better approach emerged. He runs the same twelve-month replay across three layers. For models, frontier APIs gave way to open-weight models, then bring-your-own-model, and now adaptive selection between large and small models. For agent design, single-shot LLM calls gave way to chain-of-thought, hand-built graphs, Claude-style planning agents, dedicated sub-agents with skills, agent sandboxes that execute code, and possibly user-selectable harnesses. For retrieval, BM25 gave way to RAG with embeddings and ANN, then to knowledge graphs, then to hybrid lexical-plus-semantic with rank fusion, and now to agentic search. Kus stresses none of the prior answers were wrong at the time, but each was overtaken.

Traditional infrastructure (large-scale databases, IAM, multi-cloud storage, scaling engineering teams) still changes slowly, but agent infrastructure has a half-life measured in months, not the usual three to five years. The displacement hurts engineers asked to rebuild working systems, startups whose bet is overturned, technology buyers locked into multi-year deals, and VCs whose consensus picks stop being the opportunity. Kus tells the story against himself, having shipped a working agentic search on Tuesday and then asking the team to rebuild it again on Wednesday in a newer style. He frames rapid change as a leadership, morale, and company problem: people lose faith if change looks like failure.

His prescription has three parts. First, prepare people: tell teams that change is normal and not a mistake, and that nobody knew six months ago and nobody today will know six months from now. Second, build abstractions so the layer underneath can be swapped (Box's agent abstraction lets underlying components change without breaking the customer-facing agent), and define what "change" means by switching on eval sets (cost, speed, quality, capabilities) rather than on exciting papers. Box now reviews every AI technology on a six-month clock, even though everything else is reviewed on a three-year clock. Third, recognize that nobody can keep up alone, so select vendors and platforms partly by how they have handled change; the vendors Kus trusts have reinvented themselves multiple times in the last year and built competence in evals and observability. He closes by betting that the company which will dominate tomorrow is born today, but warns its current technology approach will change multiple times before then, so adaptability is the moat, until that too changes.

takeaways: The 'pick a stack, go deep, switch rarely' playbook assumes infrastructure half-lives of three to five years; AI agent infrastructure has a half-life measured in months, which breaks the playbook.
Last year's leading agent advice (graph-based agent design) has already been superseded by newer approaches, even though it was correct when given.

Every major AI layer has churned in roughly twelve months: models (frontier → open-weight → BYO → adaptive), agent design (single-shot → CoT → graphs → planning → skills → sandbox → harnesses), and retrieval (BM25 → RAG/ANN → graphs → hybrid → agentic).
Rapid change hurts engineers, startups, technology buyers on long deals, and VCs whose consensus picks are overturned, and can destroy morale and company faith if framed as failure.

sections.title: Speaker intro and Box scale
sections.summary: Kus introduces himself as CTO of Box and frames the scale his team operates at: over an exabyte of data, tens of millions of users, hundreds of billions of content items, and now roughly a trillion tokens of AI workload, soon ten trillion.

sections.title: Why the old enterprise playbook no longer fits
sections.summary: He recounts the internet, mobile, and cloud waves and the standing advice to pick a stack, get good at it, and optimize it. That advice relied on infrastructure like HTTP, iOS, and Android persisting; generative AI's supporting layers do not, so the rate of change is dramatically higher than in prior disruptions.

sections.title: Retracting last year's graph-based agent advice
sections.summary: Kus retracts his AI Engineer talk from the prior year, which advocated a graph-based approach to agents. He recalls a grateful attendee and now wonders how that person's solution fared when a better approach emerged, illustrating that being right at the time is not enough.

sections.title: Twelve-month replay across models, agents, and retrieval
sections.summary: He runs a rapid replay of the last year. Models moved from frontier APIs to open-weight, to BYO-model, to adaptive large/small selection. Agent design moved from single-shot calls to CoT, graphs, planning agents, dedicated sub-agents with skills, sandboxed code-executing agents, and possibly user-selectable harnesses. Retrieval moved from BM25 to RAG/ANN, to knowledge graphs, to hybrid lexical-plus-semantic with rank fusion, and now to agentic search. Kus's current pick is adaptive models plus a dedicated agent with skills plus agentic search over hybrid retrieval, but flags this as unlikely to be the final answer.

sections.title: Drivers of change and what does not move this fast
sections.summary: He attributes the churn to model jumps like Opus 4.0 to 4.5, improving GPUs, soaring token usage, varied enterprise adoption strategies, and trillions of dollars of investment. He contrasts this with infrastructure domains that change slowly: large-scale databases, identity, access control, scaling engineering teams, and multi-cloud storage. He closes by restating that the 'pick a stack, switch rarely' playbook exists because migrations always break something, which still applies to traditional infra but not to agent infrastructure.

sections.title: A months-long half-life and who it hurts
sections.summary: Kus states that infrastructure usually has a three-to-five-year half-life, which is why the standard advice is to switch rarely, while agent infrastructure's half-life is measured in months. He says this is shocking and a different aspect of building technology. It hurts engineers who watch what they just learned go out of date, startups that bet on an approach only to be disrupted by the next phase, technology buyers who cannot safely sign three-year deals on AI, and VCs whose consensus opportunities shift. He frames rapid change as a leadership, morale, team, and company problem that, if mishandled, can destroy things because people lose faith.

sections.title: Get good at changing, told against himself
sections.summary: His core advice is to get good at changing. He tells a personal story: after asking an engineer to rebuild agentic search from a graph-based approach into a deep looping style, the engineer delivered a working deep research system, only for Kus to then say they would rebuild it again on yet another approach, prompting disbelief. He recounts proposing a third rebuild the day after shipping, and notes the team responds with skepticism, asking for more time, offering to squeeze more out of the current stack, and doubting the choices. He acknowledges yes, it will likely change again, and calls this a leadership problem on top of the technology problem.

sections.title: Three pieces of advice: prepare people, abstractions, eval-driven switching
sections.summary: Kus offers three pieces of advice. First, prepare people: when building AI teams, tell them change is normal and not a mistake, and that nobody knew six months ago and nobody today will know six months from now. Second, build abstractions so the layer underneath can be swapped, citing Box's agent abstraction that lets underlying components change without breaking the customer-facing agent. Define what 'change' means and don't switch on trends or exciting papers; switch when eval sets (cost, speed, quality, capabilities) say the new approach works better for what customers care about. Box now reviews every AI technology on a six-month clock, versus a three-year clock for everything else.

sections.title: Choose vendors and platforms by how they handled change
sections.summary: Kus notes that nobody can keep up with everything alone, citing Andrej Karpathy's comment about not being able to keep up, and so the answer is to rely on vendors and platforms. He updates past advice: yes, evaluate what they do now and their roadmap, but also look back at how they handled change six months and a year ago. The vendors he trusts most have reinvented themselves three times in the last year and show strength in agent technologies, eval sets, and observability, so he trusts they will keep up. He plugs Box's booth for unstructured content and AI.

sections.title: Adaptability as the moat, until that changes
sections.summary: Kus closes by betting that the company which will dominate tomorrow, whether born this year, last year, or already medium or large, is being built now, but its current technology approach will change multiple times before it gets there. Therefore, the practical advice is to build for change; adaptability is the moat a company has, on the explicit understanding that this too will change. He thanks the audience to applause.
